chunks: Every case where motors and solenoids peak. The question: When do motors/solenoids draw the most amount of current?
A motor's current is high whenever its speed is low compared to the supply voltage. That is the one rule behind every peak.
Startup, stall, a jammed shaft and a heavy load all drag the speed down. Some less obvious cases, like reversing direction, can be even worse. Solenoids peak in simpler ways.
Picture pushing a shopping cart. A cart that is already rolling away from you needs only a light push. A cart that is standing still needs a big shove.
A cart rolling toward you that you want to turn around needs the biggest effort of all, because you must stop it and push it back.
The motor's current is that effort: low speed means a lot, and reversed speed means even more.
The analogy breaks down because here the effort is electrical current, which heats the winding.
Forward (blue): maximum at standstill, falling to zero near no-load. Reversed (red): starts at about -23.
5 amps when reversed from the 575 rad/s no-load speed and rises toward -12 amps as the motor slows, then continues to spin the other way.
The orange line is dynamic braking by shorting the winding: no more than 11. 5 amps and falling linearly with speed.
The magnitude of the red line is always greater than stall (12 amps) until the motor has reversed.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply. Stall current: the current with the shaft held still, V over R .
Plugging: swapping the + and minus supply connections while the motor is still spinning.
Shoot-through: in a motor driver (the switching circuit that powers the motor), two switches turn on together and short the supply.
Current limit: a driver feature that caps the peak current.
A 12 volts motor has a 1 ohms winding and reaches 11. 5 volts of back-EMF at full speed. At stall, the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps.
Now reverse the supply at full speed. The back-EMF no longer opposes the supply but adds to it, so the voltage across the winding is 12 + 11. 5 = 23.
5 volts, and the current is 23. 5 amps , almost double stall. That is the whole idea: low speed or reversed speed means big current.
"A motor's current is V minus K e omega over R, so it peaks when speed is low relative to the supply: startup, stall, jams and heavy load, V over R, so 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm.
The biggest normal case is reversing the supply while spinning, plugging, where back-EMF adds to the supply, so about 2 volts over R, 23. 5 amps.
Shoot-through in a bridge is bigger still.
A DC solenoid peaks at V over R in steady state, or higher during a deliberate pull-in overdrive; AC solenoids have inrush with the plunger open."
